analysis.one_liner: Expands federal gun-crime prosecution, tightens background-check records, and loosens some gun sale and transport rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican bill would expand federal prosecution of gun crimes, including a "Project Exile" program in high-homicide cities, a task force for felons who try to buy guns illegally, and tougher penalties for lying on background checks and for straw purchases. It would also push federal agencies to submit their prohibiting records to the background check system and cut federal grants to states that don't report mental health records. At the same time, it loosens gun rules: dealers could sell at temporary locations in any state, people transporting firearms across state lines would be shielded from state arrest and prosecution, and people could only lose their gun rights over mental health after a formal court finding that they are dangerous.
analysis.who_benefits: Law-abiding gun owners gain clearer protection when traveling with firearms across state lines, with the government bearing the burden of proof if they are prosecuted and attorney's fees if they win. Licensed gun dealers gain the ability to sell at temporary locations like gun shows in any state. Federal prosecutors and the ATF gain roughly $25 million a year in dedicated funding for gun-crime prosecutions and trafficking task forces. People whose gun rights were stripped through administrative determinations — such as some veterans deemed incompetent by the VA without a court order — would regain rights unless a judge finds them dangerous. City residents in high-homicide areas would see more federal resources directed at armed offenders and traffickers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners, dealers, federal prosecutors, veterans

how_it_helps.text: Creates a "Nationwide Project Exile Expansion" requiring U.S. Attorneys in the 15 highest-homicide jurisdictions and 3 high-homicide Tribal jurisdictions to coordinate with local police and charge referred gun cases under the most serious federal firearms provision, with $15 million per year authorized for FY2025-2027 for new prosecutors and ATF agents [S2].

Establishes a Justice Department task force, chaired by the Deputy Attorney General, to investigate and prosecute convicted felons and fugitives who illegally attempt to buy firearms, funded at up to $10 million per year through FY2029 [S2].
Increases the maximum prison term for lying on a background check or making a straw purchase from 5 to 10 years, and extends enhanced penalties to more categories of prohibited purchasers [S2].

Requires every federal agency holding records showing someone is legally barred from buying a gun to submit those records to the background check system, and authorizes $20 million per year through FY2029 for state record-sharing grants [S2].

Lets a person transporting an unloaded, locked firearm across state lines assert a federal defense that overrides state arrest and prosecution, with the government bearing the burden of proof and the defendant collecting attorney's fees if the defense succeeds [S2].

Allows licensed dealers to sell firearms at temporary locations in any state and codifies that nothing in federal law prohibits dealer-to-dealer sales at any location, easing restrictions that previously tied dealers to their licensed state [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund roughly $45 million per year in new authorizations: $20 million for background check record grants, $15 million for prosecutors and ATF agents, and up to $10 million for the felon task force. States with strict gun laws lose some authority to arrest or prosecute people transporting firearms through their territory, and would lose 5% of their Byrne JAG policing grants, rising to 10%, if they fail to report mental health records to the background check system. People with mental health conditions could lose their gun rights only after a full court hearing with counsel and a judicial finding of danger, narrowing a prohibition that previously could rest on agency determinations — including VA competency findings — which supporters of tighter regulation say makes it easier for dangerous individuals to buy guns.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows the federal mental health gun prohibition to require a formal judicial finding with notice, a hearing, and counsel, and excludes voluntary psychiatric admissions; it also bars treating a person as prohibited based on a VA finding of incompetence unless a judge finds them dangerous, which would restore gun eligibility to some people currently barred [S2].

The rewritten interstate transport law preempts state and local firearms rules for travelers, limits when police can even arrest or detain a transporter, and puts the burden of proof on the government, which reduces the tools available to states that use strict transport laws to combat trafficking [S2].

Allowing dealers to sell at temporary locations in any state and broadening the residence rules for interstate transfers would expand points of sale across state lines, which gun trafficking researchers have long identified as a channel through which guns move from loose-regulation states into strict ones [S2].

It bars the Justice Department from running undercover sting operations against straw purchasers — where a federal licensee is directed to sell to a suspected straw buyer — unless the Attorney General or a top deputy personally approves the operation in writing, a restriction stemming from criticism of past operations like Fast and Furious that career agents say can slow investigations [S2].

The mandated mass-shooting study must examine whether perpetrators played "violent or adult-themed video games," a framing that researchers have repeatedly found does not predict mass violence, and the bill directs no comparable study of firearm access itself [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs genuinely popular measures — punishing straw buyers and lying buyers, getting prohibiting records into the background check system, and concentrating federal prosecution resources in high-homicide cities — with a significant loosening of gun rules, including easier interstate dealer sales, a narrower mental health prohibition, and preemption of state transport laws. It is a compromise package that moves both directions at once; critics of the enforcement half object to the deregulation half and vice versa. Because it never advanced, no trade-off was ever tested in a committee or on a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, killing it automatically.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on April 10, 2024, with Sens. Ted Cruz and Thom Tillis as the only cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; no further action was ever taken [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill received no committee or floor vote in either chamber [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, states with strict gun laws kept their current transport and dealer rules, the VA's administrative gun-prohibition process was left untouched, and the Justice Department kept its existing authority over undercover sting operations — while high-homicide cities also never received the extra federal prosecutors and ATF agents the bill promised. The main beneficiaries of the outcome are defenders of the regulatory status quo; the bill's only three Senate supporters gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States with strict gun laws; the status quo

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 10, 2024, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee, of which he was a senior member.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained in committee without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred; the bill's only three Senate sponsors were all Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored it, but no chamber or committee ever took a position.

industries.note: The bill lets licensed dealers sell at temporary locations in any state, broadens interstate transfer rules, and shields traveling gun owners from state arrest — expanding the industry's selling footprint and its customers' rights. The cost lands on states that use stricter rules to fight trafficking, while other sections of the same bill increase prosecution of the industry's straw-purchase customers.

industries.industry: Background check and grant administration (NICS grant program)
industries.note: The bill reauthorizes $20 million a year for state grants that improve the records feeding the background check system, but adds Inspector General audits and makes clean-audit grantees a priority, and cuts Byrne JAG funds for states that fail to report mental health records. It funds a public-safety function while tightening its accountability.
